paras: The lynching of Silas Lee was the killing of a Black farm hand by a crowd in Lincoln parish, Louisiana, about seven miles from Vienna, in July 1881. Accused by his employer's wife of being found under her young daughter's bed, Lee was shot and left for dead, then taken out again two nights later and killed. A Baton Rouge paper printed the full account under the heading "JUDGE LYNCH" and openly approved of the killing.

Lee had lived that year as a farm hand on the place of A. J. Taylor in the southern part of Lincoln parish. According to the account, Mrs. Taylor woke one Wednesday night and saw Lee lying "in a perfectly nude state" under the bed of her daughter, aged twelve or fifteen, after which he ran off.

The next night, during a Black wedding nearby, someone in the woods sent for him to help doctor a sick horse. There, the account said, a crowd met him, marched him to an old field, tied him, "literally filled" him with buckshot and left him for dead.

Lee untied himself and crawled to a nearby shanty, where a Dr. Null was called only on Saturday evening. On Saturday night he was taken out again and killed, and his body was found the next day in woods about 500 yards from A. H. Riter's place.
Coroner C. H. Griffin held an inquest where the body lay, but no verdict is reported. No arrests or named attackers appear in the coverage.

On July 30, 1881, the Louisiana Capitolian of Baton Rouge printed a long account, written from Lincoln parish, under the headings "JUDGE LYNCH" and "A Fiend Attempts to Carry out a Hellish Design." Its writer approved lynch law "when applied to cases like the present" and asserted, without detail, earlier offenses by Lee in other parishes.
The Donaldsonville Chief gave the case one sentence the same day, stating the charge as fact and reporting a single shooting in the woods by "a crowd of young men" rather than two attacks.

reader.title: Lynching of Silas Lee
bases: A crowd lured Silas Lee, accused of an offense against a white farmer's daughter, shot him and left him for dead, then took him out again two nights later and killed him, with no legal proceeding (A1, A2).

Lee was killed by 'a crowd' (A1) or 'a crowd of young men' (A2) without arrest or trial, and the account presents it as punishment for his alleged act, the editor writing that he 'pay[s] the penalty' and approving lynch law for such cases (A1).

Only two reports were found, both dated 1881-07-30; the Donaldsonville Chief's one-line item ran in a column of gleanings from the state press and probably condenses the same Lincoln parish account the Capitolian printed in full, so they are not clearly independent (A1, A2).

accounts.label: Lincoln parish account (Capitolian)
accounts.gist: Lee was found nude under the Taylor girl's bed, lured out the next night, tied and shot by a crowd and left for dead, then taken from a shanty on Saturday night and killed; the writer asserts, without support, earlier similar offenses in Ouachita and Jackson parishes.

accounts.label: State-news brief (Donaldsonville Chief)
accounts.gist: Lee attempted to outrage Taylor's daughter and was taken into the woods by a crowd of young men and shot to death, in a single episode.

framing.detail: Headlined 'JUDGE LYNCH' and 'A Fiend Attempts to Carry out a Hellish Design'; the editor said lynching was right 'in cases like the present' and that Lee's end came 'none too early'.
A one-sentence item stating the accusation as fact ('attempted to outrage') with no comment.

versions.value: Two attacks: shot and left for dead Thursday night, taken out and killed Saturday night

conflicts.note: The Capitolian's fuller, locally written account is the better evidence; the Chief's single sentence compresses events.

versions.value: Found lying nude under the daughter's bed; he fled when Mrs. Taylor screamed

conflicts.note: The Chief's wording turns Mrs. Taylor's report into a charge of attempted rape; neither paper reports any legal charge.
